# The Architecture Moonshot {#sec-moonshot}

![](images/ch01-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="A system goal leads to explicit requirements, coordinated design experiments, and evaluation of the design and the effort needed to develop it, followed by human review."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers."
>
> — Richard W. Hamming, *Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers* (1962) [@Hamming1962NumericalMethods]
:::

Architecture 2.0 asks whether learned models, connected to engineering tools and feedback, can make a broader range of hardware–software designs practical to investigate. The moonshot is to build a design system that carries a high-level goal through coordinated hardware–software exploration toward a physically realizable design. Architects set the requirements, evaluate the alternatives, and decide what to build.

This chapter develops the conceptual basis for that ambition. It distinguishes AI-assisted, AI-driven, and AI-native design workflows by how they organize the work and which architectural decisions they can revisit. Historical precedents connect advances in design expression to the tools needed to implement and check them. A running system design challenge shows how a compact request expands into requirements and architectural choices that can be evaluated.

The chapter explains how to interpret the resulting experiments and assess whether the design process improved. It distinguishes the quality of a proposed design from the effort needed to develop and check it, then examines the decisions that remain with the engineering team. These distinctions give readers a way to assess progress toward the moonshot while the complete capability remains an open research objective.

## Why AI in Architecture Design {#sec-case-for-ai-native-design}

Consider an architect asked to make a processor run a particular workload faster while staying within fixed power and chip-area limits. Increasing the amount of on-chip memory might reduce the time spent waiting for data, but that memory also occupies area and consumes power. A different organization of the computation might make better use of the existing hardware, but require changes to the software. The architect must determine which combination of choices can meet the requirements, and whether it improves on the current design.

These trade-offs have become more consequential as frequency and energy-efficiency gains from transistor scaling have diminished. Improving systems depends increasingly on parallelism, specialization, and matching hardware to software [@HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. A specialized accelerator adds choices about how to divide computation, place data, and connect components. Changes in the workload or software can require those choices to be reconsidered. Each promising combination also takes work to implement, simulate, and check. The pressures developed in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales therefore raise a practical question for architecture teams: how can they investigate enough useful alternatives, with enough confidence in the results, within the available time and budget?

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers ways to use prior designs and experimental results to guide that work.[^fn-historical-ai-c01] Learned cost models can help select which alternatives to evaluate, while models trained on code can propose implementations to investigate. Published work on tensor-program optimization and hardware-description generation provides concrete examples of these capabilities [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @VerilogEval]. The broader opportunity is to connect them to the tools and feedback used throughout an architecture study, so that an evaluation can guide the next hardware or software change. That possibility makes the organization of the design process itself a subject for architecture research.

[^fn-historical-ai-c01]: **Historical AI in Architecture**: Learning has a history both in hardware mechanisms, such as perceptron branch predictors [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron], and in design tools, such as predictive models for design-space exploration [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE]. This lecture concerns the design process, where learned components can help propose and assess changes to the hardware and software under study.

For the memory example, a generated controller or software variant is a starting point for evaluating the proposed change. A simulator can estimate how the candidate executes the workload; implementation tools can estimate whether its circuits fit within the area and power budgets. Checks are also needed to establish whether the candidate performs the intended computation correctly. Each result can change the next design choice. If a larger memory improves execution time but exceeds the power budget, the architect may revise the memory organization, change how the software uses it, or reject the candidate. Design progresses through this connection between proposing a change, checking its consequences, and deciding what to try next.

The Architecture 2.0 moonshot is to build a design system that starts from a high-level system goal and coordinates hardware–software exploration toward a physically realizable design. Such a system would use learned models to propose or assess candidates, invoke engineering tools to check them, and use the returned evidence to guide further search across hardware and software choices. Human architects would define the requirements, interpret the results, and decide which changes to pursue. The ambition extends well beyond producing a hardware description quickly.

This lecture argues that organizing a design system around these connected decisions could make a wider range of hardware–software alternatives practical to investigate. It develops a method for pursuing that possibility: make the architecture question explicit, represent the choices available to the system, connect proposed changes to engineering tools, and use their results to guide the next experiment. The complete capability remains a research ambition. Its value must be established by improving the design result, reducing the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or both, against a credible alternative. The framework gives readers a way to build and evaluate such systems as their components evolve.

## Historical Context and Design Transitions

Earlier changes in architecture practice offer useful precedents for the moonshot. Each changed how an architect expressed a design or evaluated a choice, and each depended on supporting tools and engineering practices. Their value here is to expose what a new design methodology must provide before other teams can use it reliably.

The Mead-Conway very-large-scale integration (VLSI) methodology made complex chip design more accessible through structured design rules and scalable abstractions [@MeadConway1980VLSI].[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] Designers could express layouts using a shared set of rules without handling every fabrication detail themselves. This division of work mattered as circuits grew larger: a designer needed a way to compose a system while relying on an agreed relationship between the design rules and the manufacturing process.

Reduced-instruction-set computing (RISC) connected instruction-set choices to compiler behavior and implementation cost [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. An instruction's usefulness depends on how software uses it and what the hardware must do to execute it. That relationship makes the compiler part of the architecture argument. A proposed instruction set must be judged through the programs and implementations it enables, rather than by counting its features.

Logic synthesis provides a third precedent. A register-transfer level (RTL) description expresses operations on data and registers; synthesis tools translate that description into a network of logic gates [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization]. The translation creates another object that must be checked. Formal equivalence checking can test whether the transformed implementation preserves the specified behavior, while static timing analysis (STA) checks whether signal paths satisfy declared timing constraints. Tools such as Synopsys Formality support the equivalence task [@Formality]. Producing gates and establishing that those gates meet the design's requirements are connected but distinct parts of the methodology.

Parameterized hardware generators extend this approach by encoding a family of designs. Parameters select such choices as widths, capacities, or the number of repeated blocks, and the generator produces the corresponding hardware description. Chisel provides language support for constructing such generators [@BachrachEtAl2012Chisel]. The architect still needs to evaluate the generated instance; parameterization expands what can be expressed without establishing which choice is best.

Across these examples, a useful abstraction makes a larger design problem manageable only when implementation and checking practices support it. The progression in @fig-design-method-progression links each way of expressing a design to the object it produces and the infrastructure needed to evaluate that object.

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

![**New design abstractions depend on implementation and checking tools.** The established examples connect ways of expressing a design to implementations that engineers can evaluate. The proposed design system would extend this relationship to coordinated hardware–software exploration. Its separate placement marks it as a research ambition.](images/fig-design-method-progression){#fig-design-method-progression width="90%" fig-alt="Four historical examples connect VLSI design rules, instruction-set choices, RTL, and parameterized generators to implementations and their checks. A separate proposed system connects a system goal and current design files to methods, tools, and evaluated alternatives."}

The moonshot proposes a further step in this progression. Its starting point is a system goal together with an explicit representation of the active design problem. Its tools would carry that problem through candidate generation, evaluation, and revision. Electronic design automation (EDA) checks remain essential to judging the outputs. The historical precedents motivate examining this combination; they do not establish that the proposed combination will succeed.

## Architecture 2.0 and Its Operational Layers

The historical examples connect a design abstraction to the work that tools can perform on it. This lecture distinguishes AI-assisted, AI-driven, and AI-native design workflows according to how that work is organized and which decisions the workflow can revisit. Drafting a cache controller, automatically refining it within a fixed interface, and redesigning the memory system together with its software require different forms of coordination.

Architecture spans the hardware–software contract and the organization that implements it. An architectural choice may concern the instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory, interconnects, accelerators, chiplets, compiler and runtime interfaces, or deployment model. These choices interact. A new vector unit, for example, changes what the hardware can execute, but useful performance also depends on the compiler and the workload.

Our initial paper set out the broad Architecture 2.0 vision across system and chip design [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. Architecture 2.0 concerns building and evaluating design systems that use learned components to coordinate more of this work. The three operational layers below classify the workflow as a whole, rather than the individual models or algorithms it uses.

Architects already formulate constraints, coordinate disciplines, and evaluate alternatives. The proposed change is to make more of the intervening exploration executable within the design system, including some changes that require revising hardware and software together.

### Scope of the Design Loop

The workflows differ in how the next experiment is chosen and how much of the architectural problem the system can reconsider. Assistance with a task, search within an established design formulation, and development of a different hardware–software organization place different demands on the workflow. The memory example in @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration makes these distinctions concrete.

- **L1 (AI-Assisted): Assistance with Individual Tasks.** A learned component helps with an isolated task, such as drafting RTL, preparing a test, or interpreting a tool report. The engineer or existing workflow integrates its output and determines what happens next. In our memory example, an architect might ask a generator to draft a configurable cache controller, then select the configurations and run the checks separately. The assistance changes one task within the study.
- **L2 (AI-Driven): Search and Optimization.** An automated loop selects candidates, evaluates them, and uses feedback to choose another candidate within an established design formulation. A cache optimizer might search capacities and replacement policies while preserving the processor interface and workload. Human architects define the allowed choices and constraints before search begins. The evaluator can measure effects elsewhere in the system, but the search works within that formulation. Learned macro placement, which searches positions for circuit blocks within a given design, illustrates this bounded form of optimization [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement].
- **L3 (AI-Native): Coordinated Architectural Redesign.** The workflow supports developing and evaluating alternative hardware–software organizations through coordinated use of models, engineering tools, and feedback. In our memory study, it could generate a tiled organization with a new data-transfer interface and matching software, even when the original design exposed only cache capacities as choices. It must carry that proposal through implementation and evaluation so that results can guide further redesign or refinement. Architects define the system requirements and permitted scope, and review the resulting designs. Whether the system can perform this work effectively remains a research question.

![**Design workflows differ in coordination and scope.** L1 assists an engineer with one task, L2 automates exploration within fixed interfaces, and L3 can redesign hardware and software together. The L3 example uses generation to construct a new organization and feedback to guide its revision.](images/fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration){#fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration width="90%" fig-alt="L1 drafts a controller for an engineer. L2 uses feedback to select cache configurations. L3 generates a new tiled organization, implements matching hardware and software, and evaluates it, with feedback returning to design generation and revision."}

Prediction, generation, and optimization are methods that can operate within any of these workflows. A predictor estimates a candidate's behavior or cost, a generator constructs a candidate or artifact, and an optimizer searches for choices that improve a stated objective. An agent is a software component that reads feedback and selects its next permitted action without a human choosing each intervening step. These methods and components can be combined according to the design question; they do not correspond one-to-one with the three layers. Method selection and composition are developed in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization.

For example, generating a controller for an engineer is an L1 task. A loop that generates, checks, and revises the controller within its fixed interface is an L2 workflow. An L3 workflow can use generation to develop a different memory organization together with matching software. That organization may combine familiar architectural ideas. A novel proposal or permission to change an interface does not by itself establish the additional capability: the workflow must carry the coordinated change through implementation and evaluation. The layers describe different kinds of work, and a well-defined optimization problem may be best served by an L2 workflow.

### Coordinating Actions and Tool Feedback

Broader scope is valuable when a useful alternative requires several choices to change together. Consider a hypothetical accelerator whose interface requires an entire input array to reside in on-chip memory before computation begins. If we hold that interface fixed, an input larger than the available memory may force a capacity increase that exceeds the area budget. Another organization could process the input in smaller tiles, but it would need matching changes to software scheduling, data transfers, and the accelerator's handling of partial results. A capacity-only search cannot propose that combination because the necessary interface changes lie outside its allowed choices.

An architect can already devise this alternative. The AI-native opportunity is for the design system to generate and evaluate such alternatives as the study proceeds. A generator might construct the tiled organization and its matching interface and software, while an optimizer selects tile sizes within it. If evaluation exposes excessive transfer overhead, the returned results could guide generation of a different buffering or transfer organization. The tiled candidate could still lose its apparent advantage to that overhead or extra control logic. Evaluating the trade-off requires a working hardware–software combination, which gives the loop in @fig-architecture-20-loop a concrete purpose.

![**Tool feedback guides design generation and revision.** In this proposed loop, a generator constructs a candidate organization and matching hardware and software. Engineering tools evaluate its behavior and implementation. Results guide the next proposal and remain available for architect review.](images/fig-architecture-20-loop){#fig-architecture-20-loop width="90%" fig-alt="Requirements guide generation of a candidate organization, implementation of matching hardware and software, and engineering evaluations. Measurements and failures return to design generation and remain available for architect review."}

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

The arrows returning from the tools carry more than a pass or fail. Suppose a candidate reduces simulated execution time, but an implementation tool reports that signals cannot traverse a critical path within the allowed clock period. That timing failure may rule out the current implementation or motivate a different pipeline organization. It does not, by itself, identify a correct repair. An automated component needs enough information about the candidate, constraints, and failing path to choose a meaningful next experiment. Representing this information without losing its engineering meaning is one of the challenges developed in @sec-data-representations-world-models.

Each experiment can therefore change both the candidate and the direction of the search. Making those iterations executable requires work of its own: preparing interfaces, maintaining consistent hardware and software versions, and interpreting tool failures. The opportunity must be assessed together with that cost.

The memory example identifies a reason to investigate broader search, but a useful design must satisfy more than one local constraint. A concrete system challenge can expose how workload behavior, software choices, and physical limits interact throughout the exploration.


## The Lighthouse XR System-on-Chip (SoC) Case Study

We use the name *Lighthouse* for the running design challenge through which this lecture develops and examines AI-native design workflows. The challenge is to develop a mobile extended-reality (XR) compute subsystem that executes perception and rendering workloads within a wearable device's power limits. Computation, memory, software, and physical implementation all affect whether it can do so. The shared problem gives each chapter a concrete setting in which to develop its ideas. This edition presents a prospective study; it does not report a completed Lighthouse implementation.

An engineering milestone can make progress visible even when its first attempts fail. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Grand Challenge offers a useful precedent: no vehicle completed the 2004 route, while five completed the 132\ mile desert course in 2005 [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley]. The relevant lesson is the value of a shared task with an observable outcome. Lighthouse proposes such a task for architecture, where generating an implementation is only one part of reaching an independently checkable result.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{7\baselineskip}
```

> **The Lighthouse goal.** Demonstrate by 2030 that an AI-native design system can develop a compact system request into candidate implementations spanning software, microarchitecture, and physical design, quantify their power, performance, and area (PPA) trade-offs, and produce an implementation that meets the agreed system requirements and passes physical signoff.

The XR setting makes those trade-offs tangible. A frame delivered after its deadline can harm the experience even if average throughput is high, and a short performance burst does not establish sustained operation within a thermal limit. XRBench supplies a suite of mobile XR workloads for studying these dependencies [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]; ILLIXR connects the broader XR experience to its computational components [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. These dependencies make Lighthouse a useful test of coordination. A change that reduces memory traffic must still fit the software's execution schedule and the device's sustained power budget. The study can expose whether the design system follows those consequences across domains. Success would support the approach for the workloads, tools, and design choices examined; transfer to other architecture problems would remain a separate question.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse}
Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload. The implementation may use a vector-capable central processing unit (CPU), an accelerator, or a system-on-chip (SoC) block. It must target a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope in a 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process.

Return a design-space report that explains which candidates were tested, how they compared, and which design the team should investigate further.
:::

The prompt is short because it leaves many decisions unstated. It names a workload class and physical targets, but it does not determine the processor organization, the memory hierarchy, or how software should use them. The eight domains in @fig-moonshot-prompt expose these missing decisions and connect them to the tools needed to evaluate a proposed design.

![**A compact request leaves many architectural decisions open.** The Lighthouse prompt expands into eight coupled domains. Choices in those domains determine which workload simulations, implementation tools, and verification checks are needed to evaluate a candidate.](images/fig-moonshot-prompt){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="80%" fig-alt="The Lighthouse prompt expands into workload, ISA and ABI, compute, memory, power, software, process, and verification decisions, which feed design experiments and engineering review."}

The domains should be read as questions an architect must answer, rather than as a completed specification. The prompt supplies the XR workload class, 64-bit RISC-V basis, 3\ W target, and 3\ nm-class process. The choices below illustrate one possible expansion. A study would distinguish supplied requirements from added assumptions, then declare which choices are fixed and which remain searchable.

1. **Workload domain.** Identify the XRBench workloads, inputs, and scenarios whose behavior the candidate must support [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. A design that handles one sequence of perception and rendering tasks may behave differently when their rates or overlap change.
2. **ISA and ABI contract domain.** Choose the instruction extensions and the application binary interface (ABI), the conventions that allow compiled software to call functions and exchange data.[^fn-abi-c01] Supporting the RISC-V vector extension, for example, is an additional design choice [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. It does not follow automatically from the request for a 64-bit RISC-V subsystem.
3. **Compute organization domain.** Determine whether the workload should run on a vector-capable CPU, a neural processing unit (NPU), or a combination. An NPU organized as a systolic array passes data through a regular arrangement of processing elements; its benefit depends on whether the workload and software can use that arrangement effectively.
4. **Memory and data movement domain.** Choose capacities, interfaces, and data placement. An illustrative starting point uses a 32\ KiB L1 cache, a 2\ MiB L2 cache, and a 4\ MiB shared L3 cache, plus tightly coupled memory (TCM) scratchpads. The study could vary the L2 capacity while holding the other capacities fixed. Increasing capacity may reduce external memory traffic, but also changes the memory's area, access time, and power. The evaluation must account for both effects within the subsystem's 3\ W budget.
5. **Power envelope domain.** Define what the 3\ W target covers and how long it must be sustained. Passive cooling through the frame and a skin-temperature ceiling below $41^\circ\text{C}$ are additional illustrative assumptions. A thermal model must test whether the proposed package and operating conditions make them compatible.[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01]
6. **Compiler and runtime stack domain.** Establish how software maps useful work onto the selected hardware. A proposed 120\ frames per second (FPS) operating point gives roughly 8.33\ ms per frame; the workload scenario must determine which stages share that deadline and how their execution overlaps [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. A new vector unit or accelerator cannot improve this path unless software can use it.
7. **Physical constraints domain.** Select a specific implementation process, cell libraries, and operating conditions. The phrase “3\ nm-class” identifies a technology target, but does not supply the process-specific information that implementation and signoff tools require.
8. **Reliability and verification domain.** State the behaviors and operating conditions the checks must cover. Correct computation, interface protocols, clock timing, and transitions between power states need different checks. The required checks depend on which parts of the design the experiment changes.

[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01]: **Mobile XR and Smart Glasses Thermal Boundaries**: A power target alone does not determine the temperature of a wearable surface. Heat paths through the package and frame, ambient conditions, and duration of operation affect the temperature where the device contacts skin. The $41^\circ\text{C}$ value here is an illustrative study assumption, not a universal safety threshold or proof that 3\ W can be dissipated comfortably. Process, packaging, memory, and interconnect choices must be evaluated within the chosen form factor.

These domains interact through concrete interfaces. If an accelerator uses the Arm Advanced Microcontroller Bus Architecture (AMBA) Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) protocol, its controller must obey the transfer rules even when the receiver cannot accept more data [@Arm2020AXI]. This on-chip communication protocol is separate from the processor's instruction set. Backpressure is the receiver's way of making the sender wait. A candidate that ignores it might appear fast in a test that never exercises waiting, yet lose data or stall when other components contend for memory. The specification and tests must cover that interaction before the apparent speedup can be treated as an improvement.

The eight domains establish the breadth of the Lighthouse problem. A capacity sweep can answer a useful question within an existing memory organization. The broader opportunity is to investigate whether a different organization, with matching data transfers and software, better satisfies the same system requirements. A single experiment need not search all eight domains at once. The architect must choose which uncertainty to investigate, fix enough of the surrounding system to interpret the answer, and leave the relevant design choices open. That decision turns the broad challenge into work that tools can execute.

## Decomposing Intent into Executable Specifications {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

An executable specification connects a selected architecture question to the inputs, configurations, and checks that tools need to evaluate candidates. Suppose a Lighthouse study asks whether changing memory organization and software tiling together can meet the workload deadline within the power budget. The eight domains in @fig-moonshot-prompt identify the surrounding decisions; the specification records which of them this experiment fixes and which it investigates. It also defines the observations that could answer the question.

For this illustrative study, five decisions connect the question to an executable comparison.

1. **Bind the comparison to a workload and required behavior.** Select an XRBench scenario, its inputs, and the software behavior candidates must preserve. A reference implementation supplies the comparison point. Tiling may change the order of computation and data transfers, so the checks must establish that the resulting outputs still meet the workload's correctness requirements. If the study uses the illustrative 120\ Hz operating point, it must identify which work falls within each 8.33\ ms frame deadline and how concurrent stages share the available resources.
2. **Declare the changes the experiment permits.** Memory capacity, tile dimensions, and the accelerator's data-transfer interface might vary together while the instruction set and the application-visible behavior remain fixed. Each candidate must include the matching software and interface checks. The AXI transfer rules still apply wherever that protocol is retained. The compiler must be able to generate code for the revised hardware interface; adding or changing its translation rules becomes part of the study's development work. The verification discussion in @sec-feedback-verification-trust examines how checks must follow the changes allowed by a search.
3. **Make the limits operational.** Declare which components the 3\ W budget covers, the workload activity used to estimate power, and the duration over which the limit must hold. A candidate cannot appear to save power by moving transfers or computation outside that accounting boundary. Keep the process and operating conditions comparable, and account for the area, leakage, and access-time consequences of changing memory capacity. If the illustrative surface-temperature limit is also required, evaluate it with a thermal model. The physical constraints developed in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales explain why these consequences can determine which organization is feasible.
4. **Match the evaluation tools to the question.** Workload simulation can compare execution time and memory traffic, while implementation tools estimate the area and timing consequences of the proposed memory and controller changes. Physical evaluation needs a foundry process design kit (PDK),[^fn-pdk-c01] characterized libraries, and declared operating conditions. The software and interface checks must also cover the revised design. A faster simulated execution would have little value if tiling changed the computed answer or the controller lost data during a transfer.
5. **Specify the alternatives and the stopping conditions.** Compare the joint change with the reference design and with credible alternatives that change only memory capacity or only software tiling, where those alternatives are legal. This helps reveal whether coordinating the changes adds value. Report which candidates satisfy the limits and which trade-offs remain. Among the evaluated feasible candidates, the Pareto frontier retains those for which no other candidate improves one objective without worsening another [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. A declared search and evaluation budget bounds how much work the study can spend before returning a finding or identifying an unresolved question.

[^fn-abi-c01]: **Application binary interface (ABI)**: The conventions for register usage, calling sequences, stack layout, and data representation that allow separately compiled software to interoperate. Instruction-set support and binary compatibility are related but distinct requirements.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **Process design kit (PDK)**: The package for one manufacturing process that supplies device models, design rules, and related data used by implementation tools. The open SKY130 PDK demonstrates that a PDK can be published [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], but it cannot supply the authorized project-specific information for a different process or commercial tool flow.

These decisions preserve room for exploration while making each candidate comparable. The experiment may identify a useful joint change, find that a simpler alternative suffices, or finish without finding a candidate that meets the requirements. Establishing that no feasible design exists requires stronger evidence than exhausting the study budget. Demonstrating that an AI-native design system investigates the question more effectively requires accounting for the work used to propose, implement, and check the candidates.

Point AI assistance can help extract candidate constraints from documents, identify inconsistent units, or surface an ambiguous deadline. The architect must validate the proposed interpretation before tools use it. A model asked to propose the next candidate then needs the accepted requirements, the current hardware and software, and the results of earlier tests. Supplying that information is part of the design system's work.

## AI Models vs. AI-Native Design Systems

A learned model and a design system have different jobs. A model may propose a controller, predict a candidate's power, or rank configurations worth evaluating. To perform a useful task, it needs the relevant inputs from the current study. Its learned parameters do not, by themselves, identify which workload trace, tool version, or power budget belongs to the experiment.

An architecture foundation model is a pretrained learned component that can be adapted or supplied with context for several architecture tasks [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels]. Its reusable capabilities may help generate code, estimate performance, or interpret a report. The surrounding design system connects those capabilities to the particular hardware, software, and tools being used. It may also use specialized predictors and conventional search methods where those are more suitable.

For the Lighthouse memory experiment, the system must supply a candidate's matching hardware and software, configure the simulator with the chosen workload, and associate the returned measurements with that configuration. It must then make those results available when selecting the next experiment. The relationships in @fig-foundation-system explain why improving a model alone does not supply all of this functionality.

![**A model contributes to an experiment run by the surrounding design system.** The current requirements, design versions, and tool configurations supply the context for proposals and evaluations. Learned and conventional methods use the returned results to select further experiments. Reusable knowledge in a model remains separate from the inputs and results of the current study [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20].](images/fig-foundation-system){#fig-foundation-system width="90%" fig-alt="Requirements, matching hardware and software versions, and tool settings provide inputs to learned or conventional methods and engineering tools. Results are saved with the candidate that produced them and can guide the next experiment. A foundation model is one optional component."}

Suppose a larger cache appears to improve execution time. To interpret the comparison, we need to know whether it ran the same workload trace as the reference, under the same relevant assumptions, and with matching software. A model's summary that the cache was “faster” cannot answer those questions without the underlying experiment information. The files and results must remain available for an engineer to check the comparison.

New candidates and tool settings should therefore be saved as new versions. Replacing a model should likewise preserve which model and inputs produced earlier proposals when that affects the comparison. This lets the team test whether a change to the model or the surrounding software improved the work, while still being able to reproduce and interpret its earlier experiments.

## Interpreting Design Results

With the workload, software, and tool settings preserved, another engineer can revisit an experiment. Interpreting its results requires connecting the measurements to the original design question. In the Lighthouse study, the question is whether a memory-and-software change meets the workload deadline within the power and area limits. Each evaluation answers part of that question.

Suppose a larger cache reduces execution time in simulation, but its implementation exceeds the available area. The experiment has explained why that candidate does not meet the requirements. The team may retain the reference design, try a different memory organization, or investigate whether software tiling can reduce the required capacity. Reporting only the simulated speedup would hide the result that determines what to try next.

### What the Evaluations Establish

A candidate is the design or configuration being evaluated. The tools produce artifacts such as executable code, a gate-level netlist, a layout, or a report, together with measurements and check results. The architectural result is what the team can conclude from them about the design question. That conclusion may favor one candidate, reject the alternatives tested, or leave the question unresolved. It must remain clear whether a reported value came from a learned estimate, a simulator, an implementation tool, or a physical measurement.

Evaluation can proceed from inexpensive screening to more detailed checks. Analytical bounds can reject a proposed target that exceeds what the stated assumptions permit. Amdahl's law bounds the effect of accelerating part of a workload [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. The Roofline model connects useful operations per byte transferred, or operational intensity, to limits imposed by compute throughput and memory bandwidth [@Williams2009Roofline]. These models help identify candidates worth evaluating more closely; their conclusions remain conditional on the workload and model assumptions. A candidate that survives screening still needs the checks required for the next decision. Simulation can establish a performance difference under its assumptions, while readiness for fabrication requires physical signoff.

A surrogate model provides another form of inexpensive screening by approximating an outcome that would otherwise require a costly evaluation [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. For example, an estimated power value could help select cache configurations for implementation. The estimate addresses one property of the design. A search that ranks candidates by predicted power while omitting routing checks might favor densely packed memory blocks that cannot be routed successfully.[^fn-overfitting-c01] More detailed implementation checks can expose that failure and redirect the search.

[^fn-overfitting-c01]: **Overfitting and Proxy Exploitation**: The machine-learning failure of fitting the noise of a training sample so closely that performance does not generalize to new data [@HastieTibshiraniFriedman2009Elements]. Proxy exploitation is analogous but distinct; it occurs when search algorithms exploit omissions or modeling errors in an evaluator, embodying Goodhart's law in automated design [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement].

The checks themselves also need scrutiny. A generated accelerator and a testbench written from the same mistaken interpretation may agree while both violate the intended behavior. The Knight–Leveson multiversion experiment illustrates why separate implementations do not automatically provide independent checks [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. For the tiled accelerator, a test that checks each tile separately could miss an error in how partial results are combined. The verification methods in @sec-feedback-verification-trust develop this issue further. In reporting the experiment, the team must explain which required behaviors its checks covered and which remain untested.

### Design Quality and Engineering Effort {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

The same candidate can look attractive under one measure and unattractive under another. For the XR subsystem, improving frame latency may require more memory capacity or greater power. System evaluation must account for these consequences within the chosen subsystem [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. A throughput improvement does not by itself establish that the design meets the other requirements.

Memory traffic gives a concrete example. An accelerator could reduce the energy spent on arithmetic while increasing transfers to off-chip dynamic random-access memory (DRAM). Those transfers also consume energy. For Lighthouse, the relevant comparison includes the complete workload execution within the chosen power budget. The reference energy comparisons in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales develop this issue quantitatively.

There is also a separate cost to finding and checking the candidate. Simulation time, tool licenses, failed experiments, and human review belong to the engineering effort, rather than to the candidate's operating energy. A method might find a better design at greater expense, or reach a comparable design more cheaply. Reporting both makes it possible to judge whether the method helped.

The same accounting applies to time. If drafting accounts for a small share of the schedule, faster drafting alone has limited effect on when the design is ready. Amdahl's law makes that limit explicit.

::: {.callout-law title="Amdahl's Law for Semiconductor Teams"}
**The classical principle.** If a fraction $f$ of the original work is accelerated by a factor $s$ and the rest is unchanged, the overall speedup is $S = \frac{1}{(1-f) + f/s}$ [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. The expression assumes that the original allocation remains applicable and that the acceleration introduces no additional overhead.

**An illustrative design schedule.** Suppose RTL drafting accounts for $15\%$ of elapsed time in a sequential design schedule, while testing, implementation, and review account for the other $85\%$. Even instantaneous drafting leaves that remaining work. Under this assumed split, the maximum speedup is $S_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{1-0.15} = 1.176\times$. A real project must measure its own allocation, including any changes in downstream checking effort. When tasks overlap, the analysis must identify which tasks actually determine the completion time.

**The architectural consequence.** Larger gains require reducing work outside drafting or changing the workflow itself. Coordinating hardware and software changes is one possible way to improve the search, but building and checking that coordination also takes work. The broader workflow interpretation is developed in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes.
:::

To test whether the approach helps with Lighthouse, a comparison would give a conventional team the same task, tool access, and engineering budget. Both approaches would be assessed using criteria chosen before the searches began, including acceptable measurement differences. The comparison must account for the effort spent preparing the design system as well as running it. Otherwise, moving work into model adaptation, tool integration, or test development could look like a saving when it merely occurred outside the reported experiment.

These distinctions let us assess published work with two concrete questions: what design task did the method perform, and what did its evaluation establish about the resulting design or the effort required? A method can make a useful contribution without carrying out the whole Lighthouse study.

## What Published Systems Demonstrate {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

Learned macro placement and hardware-description generation illustrate two capabilities that a broader design system might use. Examining what each method changes and how its outputs were evaluated helps locate its contribution to the larger design problem.

Learned macro placement searches locations for circuit blocks within an existing design [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. It addresses an implementation choice whose quality matters to the resulting chip. Under the operational layers defined earlier, placement search within a fixed design is an L2 capability. Its evaluation concerns the choices available within that boundary; it does not evaluate whether the system should change its memory organization or software interface. In a broader workflow, placement feedback could help assess such a change, but another part of the system would have to propose and carry it through implementation.

VerilogEval makes a different contribution by defining programming tasks and functional checks for generated hardware descriptions [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]. Its code-completion and specification-to-RTL tasks let researchers evaluate whether a model can supply a candidate that passes those checks. Pass@1 estimates the chance that one generated candidate passes under the specified generation and evaluation conditions. That is useful evidence when choosing a generator for a design system. The score alone does not describe the enclosing workflow's operational layer or establish that its outputs meet physical constraints.

Together, these examples make part of the proposed approach concrete. A design system could use generation to construct alternatives and bounded optimization to improve their implementations. The remaining integration question is how it would choose useful changes across domains, supply consistent inputs to each tool, and use returned evidence to select the next experiment. Successful components establish opportunities for that composition; the complete workflow needs its own evaluation.

Using these components also requires decisions about what they may change. A placement method can rearrange blocks within a fixed design; a system that proposes a different memory organization may affect software, power, and product requirements. The team must decide which changes belong inside the experiment and which require further review.

## Human Review and Design Decisions {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

An automated search may request another simulation or power estimate within the experiment the architect has defined. Changing the product's requirements is a different decision. Permission to compare memory configurations within a 3\ W budget does not include permission to raise that budget when the search fails to find a suitable design.

Consider a Lighthouse candidate that reduces simulated memory traffic but has not completed power or timing checks. The system can retain it for further investigation and schedule those evaluations. If the completed checks expose a conflict, it can investigate repairs or alternative organizations within the permitted scope. The architect must judge whether the resulting alternatives answer the original question or call for reconsidering the product target. That judgment depends on the purpose of the system as well as the tool reports.

The architect is responsible for combining these observations into a design recommendation. Specialists assess the measurements and perform the technical signoffs in their domains. The people responsible for the product decide whether to accept a requirement change or authorize fabrication. The architect may also hold that responsibility, but the team must know who can approve each decision. Automation can organize the analysis and propose alternatives while these responsibilities remain with people.

Human review should therefore address the design reasoning. If the system recommends a larger memory, the architect should be able to examine why software tiling or a simpler controller was rejected, whether the workload comparison is fair, and which implementation limits remain unresolved. A list of successful tool runs cannot answer those questions on its own. The account of the architect's work in @sec-what-architect-owns develops how to maintain that technical involvement as more experiments become automated.

## Assessing Progress Toward the Moonshot

The Lighthouse milestone, the value of the design method, and the decision to manufacture a product answer different questions. Keeping them separate makes it possible to recognize progress without changing the goal after an experiment finishes.

The stated Lighthouse milestone is to develop the compact request into an implementation that meets the agreed system requirements and passes physical signoff by 2030. The demonstration must also show which design decisions the system made and which required human intervention. It would establish capability for the workloads, tools, and design choices examined. A study that rejects every candidate can still teach something useful, but it has not completed that implementation milestone.

Establishing the value of the approach requires the comparison described above. Did it find a better design, reduce the total effort needed to reach a comparable result, or both? Matching a conventional team's result at the same cost demonstrates an alternative way to do the work. Improving the result or reducing its cost provides evidence for adopting that alternative. The broader Architecture 2.0 argument depends on such advantages, whose extent and transfer to other problems remain to be established.

Approval to manufacture is a further engineering and business decision. It depends on physical signoff, product requirements, cost, schedule, and the risks the organization is prepared to accept. A useful design method may produce a design the team chooses not to fabricate. Conversely, a design may be worth building even if the automated method used to find it proved more expensive than the conventional approach. Evaluating the method and deciding what to build require related information, but neither decision settles the other.

## How the Book Develops the Argument

Pursuing the moonshot requires understanding both the architecture problem and the process used to investigate it. The chapters follow that dependency, building toward an assessment of what a complete AI-native design system can accomplish. The discussion assumes familiarity with basic computer architecture. Concepts from machine learning, verification, and physical design are developed where they become necessary to the argument.

The starting point is the work an architect needs help with. The scaling limits and compounding design pressures in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales explain why assistance is worth investigating and why faster candidate generation may leave the dominant costs untouched. The design life cycle in @sec-architecture-20-ontology then organizes an architecture question into a study, connecting its formulation to experiments, interpretation, and a decision. Together, these chapters establish what the work is for before asking which methods should perform it.

Carrying out that study requires a representation of the problem, a choice of methods, and access to useful feedback. Data and representations in @sec-data-representations-world-models determine which design choices and constraints a method can use. Prediction, generation, and optimization in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization provide different ways to act on that information. The execution environments in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces connect those methods to engineering tools; verification and feedback in @sec-feedback-verification-trust determine what can be learned from the results. This sequence explains how the parts depend on one another, including why a promising method can fail when its data, tools, or checks are inadequate.

The worked study in @sec-running-the-loop examines parts of this process through bounded comparisons, distinguishing the prospective Lighthouse path from the separate executed example and making clear where the available evidence stops. The transfer analysis in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack asks which lessons remain useful when the workload, toolchain, or design problem changes. System evaluation in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect then tests the complete approach against alternatives, including the costs of obtaining and checking its results. A successful local example becomes a starting point for these comparisons, rather than sufficient evidence of general capability.

Technical evaluation still leaves decisions for people and institutions. The architect's responsibilities in @sec-what-architect-owns connect experimental results to decisions about what to build and when it is ready. The ecosystem discussion in @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem examines the shared tools, benchmarks, and research practices needed to make this work repeatable beyond one team. The aim is to equip readers to reason about when AI earns a place in architecture design, when conventional methods are preferable, and when the evidence is insufficient to decide. Several difficulties introduced here remain open even with that broader account of the work.

## Open Questions

Each chapter closes with open questions about the ideas it develops. For the introduction, the central uncertainty is whether models, tools, and feedback can be combined into a design process that is more effective than the alternatives. The examples expose four connected difficulties, from interpreting the initial request to deciding whether the resulting search was worthwhile.

- **How should a design system handle an incomplete specification?** Lighthouse leaves many choices open, as any compact request must. Some choices can be explored freely, while others change the intended product. Different interpretations may all pass the available checks. The difficulty is recognizing when the missing information matters enough to ask the architect, especially when an assumption becomes consequential only after several hardware and software changes. Resolving that uncertainty is part of the design process, not merely a preliminary parsing task.

- **Can a design system discover useful organizations beyond its starting templates?** A cache-capacity sweep can select a capacity, but it cannot introduce a cache if its representation contains no such choice. Generative methods could propose memory organizations and matching interfaces that the original template cannot express. The system must still determine whether those organizations can be implemented and checked. The open problem is how to combine architectural knowledge with enough freedom to find useful structures, while keeping the resulting exploration tractable.

- **How can evaluation feedback guide the next architectural change?** An implementation tool may identify a failing timing path without establishing whether the best response is a local repair, a different pipeline, or a change to the software interface. Those alternatives have consequences that the original report does not measure. More detailed evaluation can help distinguish them, but competes for the budget available to investigate other designs. The question is how a design system can use partial results to select productive next experiments without repeatedly favoring changes that exploit a model's omissions.

- **When does architectural redesign justify its additional cost?** Developing a different hardware–software organization can open useful alternatives, but requires building and checking more of the system. Strong coupling between architectural decisions may make coordinated redesign valuable. In other problems, optimizing within an existing organization may recover most of the benefit. The research question is which properties of a design problem predict that difference, and whether those properties can be identified before the team invests in a broader system.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{36\baselineskip}
```

## Summary

The memory-and-tiling example shows how a design question can lead from tuning an existing organization to developing a different one. An AI-native workflow must support the resulting hardware and software changes together and use evaluation to guide further work. Lighthouse turns that opportunity into a concrete challenge, connecting a compact request to requirements, experiments, and physical implementation. Its 2030 implementation milestone remains an ambition. Establishing the wider value of the approach requires showing which designs work and whether the process improves on credible alternatives.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Match the workflow to the problem.** AI-assisted workflows help with tasks; AI-driven workflows automate search within an established formulation; AI-native workflows support coordinated architectural redesign. The broader workflow is useful when the design question requires it.
- **Separate workflows from methods.** Prediction, generation, and optimization can contribute at every layer. Generating a new artifact alone does not establish an AI-native design capability.
- **Make the experiment interpretable.** Specify what may change, preserve the inputs and configurations, and explain what each evaluation establishes about the design.
- **Assess the design and the method.** Compare both design quality and total engineering effort with a credible conventional approach. A better candidate can still come from a more expensive process.
- **Keep people involved in the engineering decisions.** Architects formulate the problem and interpret the alternatives. The people responsible for the product decide whether to change its requirements or proceed to fabrication.
:::

@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales explains why reaching a result of this kind has become difficult, which pressures are decisive, and where assistance might help.
